"You're missing the game," Foster said, standing over her with the basketball. "We can play under the lights by the courts."

"One row," Charlie said. "Then I'll come for half an hour." She struck a match and the flame took, and her cousin gave a small cheer, and she realized she was not doing this only out of obligation. There was something in the doing itself, the plain arithmetic of it: darkness arrived, and you put a flame against it, and if the wind came back you did it again. She thought of her uncle, who at funerals always stood up to eulogize the dead in a language she half understood, and how he did that the same way he did this, steadily, without asking whether it would hold.

"Who taught you to do that?" Sidney asked, crouching beside her.

"A nine-year-old pedagogue," Charlie said, nodding at her cousin, who was now lecturing Foster on wick length with the plywood shield still raised like a professor's pointer. Foster laughed so hard he had to sit down on the cold ground, and Charlie's mother, hearing him, almost smiled.

At seven-thirty Charlie played twenty minutes of basketball under the montane air that had swept down and made everyone's breath visible, and at eight she came back, because the guests were arriving and the rows needed tending. She stood with her mother when the last diya was lit and someone's phone played music and the pavilion glowed like something afloat. Sidney and Foster stayed, unasked, eating a second round of jalebi, and Foster asked whether the courts would be open next weekend, and Charlie said probably, and her cousin tugged her sleeve and said, "Some of them went out again," and pointed to the far row, where three small flames were already curled and dying in the wind. She took out the matches.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A Danish study published in 2019 followed more than 650,000 children and found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism, even among children with autistic siblings.
story:
Hayden set his phone face down beside his plate before his mother could say anything about it, which was itself a kind of announcement. Across the table his father was sawing through a pork chop and saying, for the third time since Tuesday, that he wasn't sure about the whole vaccine thing anymore, that a guy at the plant had shown him a video where a doctor explained it all, that twelve kids got sick right after their shots and nobody wanted to talk about it.

"Twelve kids," Hayden said. "Where's that from?"

"From the study, Hayden. The original one. Twelve children." His father pointed his fork at him the way he pointed at everything, gently, but with the whole arm behind it. "You're telling me twelve kids counts for nothing?"

"It's not that it counts for nothing." Hayden heard himself pause, and in the pause he could feel the shape of the argument he'd been half-building since Mr. Holloway's class that morning, where Elsa had stood up and said the words badly and been laughed at for them. "It's that twelve is twelve. If I flip a coin twelve times and it comes up heads nine times, does that mean the coin's rigged?"

His mother said, "This again," but she said it toward the gravy boat, not toward either of them, which Hayden had learned to read as permission.

"There's a Danish study," he went on. "Published in 2019. It followed more than 650,000 children." He said the number slowly, because Elsa had said it slowly that morning, stumbling on it, and Mr. Holloway had let her finish before the boy in the second row, Brent, started in about how you could find a study to prove anything these days. "And it found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Not a small link. None. Even among kids who had autistic siblings, which is the group you'd most expect to show it if it was there."

"Even among," his father repeated, in the tone he used for things he suspected of being too neat. "Who wrote it, Denmark? You trust Denmark?"

"I trust a study that followed 650,000 kids more than I trust a video your friend from the plant found," Hayden said, and immediately wished he'd softened it, because his father put the fork down.

For a moment the only sounds were his mother serving green beans and the refrigerator cycling on in the kitchen. Then his father said, "Your Uncle Ray was furloughed that spring, you know. Six weeks. And the doctors couldn't tell him a thing about his hip, not one thing, just shrugs. So don't sit there and tell me the science always knows."

That was the part Hayden hadn't worked out before dinner. There were two different conversations happening, and he had been trying to win the wrong one. The science didn't always know, that was true; his father had watched it not know, up close, in a season when everything else was falling apart too. He thought about Mr. Holloway that morning, how he hadn't rescued Elsa, how he'd only said, "How would we check?" and let the room sit with it. How Brent had said, "You can't check everything," and Elsa had said, "No, but you can check this," and the checking was the whole point, or most of it.

"It's not that it always knows," Hayden said. "It's that it found out. That's what the study is, Dad. It's a bunch of people who didn't just trust the first answer, they went and looked at 650,000 children, and other people looked at how they did it, and other people ran it again. It's not one guy with a video. It's the opposite of one guy with a video." He turned his glass a quarter turn on the tablecloth. "I'm not saying the twelve kids never existed. I'm saying twelve isn't enough to know from, and the people who did the big study knew that too, so they did the big study."

His father was quiet, chewing, looking at the middle of the table. When Hayden was younger, his father had been the loud one at every gathering, the uncle who got obstreperous after two beers and had to be walked out to the porch, and Hayden had loved him and dreaded him in nearly equal measure. Now he just looked tired, like a man who had been handed a lot of hard things in the last few years and had started grabbing whatever was nearby to hold onto.

"Six hundred and fifty thousand," his father said at last.

"More than that. Six-fifty-plus."

His mother passed his father the rolls, which he hadn't asked for, and he took one. "Send me the thing," he said. "The study, not some kid yelling about it on the internet. The actual thing. I'll read it on break."

"Tonight," Hayden said. "I'll text you the link right now, actually, because I've got it pulled up." He turned the phone over. Elsa had sent it to him after class with a single message, "you said it better than I did," which wasn't true but which he had read three times anyway.

"Chew first," his mother said, and Hayden put the phone back down, picked up his fork, and finished the pork chop before he typed anything.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Nicholas arrived eleven minutes early, which was typical of him, and which meant eleven minutes alone in Ms. Kang's studio with the lid of the grand piano open. He set his bag by the door, sat down on the bench, and, because he could not yet play anything worth hearing, he counted. His finger hovered above the keys without touching them, the way you might trace words in a book you hadn't learned to read. At the top end the keys shrank into the case, and he lost his place somewhere in the middle, so he started over, this time counting only the white ones. Fifty-two. Then the black ones, gathered in their little twos and threes. Thirty-six. He added the numbers in his head. Eighty-eight. He sat with that for a moment, oddly moved, as if the instrument had confessed something to him.

He had wanted this for most of a year, since the night his grandmother's records came out of the attic and he heard the Goldberg variations for the first time. His father thought lessons were a fine idea in principle and a questionable one now, with tuition bills four months away. "Learn it in college," his father had said, which Nicholas understood to mean never. So he was paying for the lessons himself, out of a summer of bagging groceries, and the money was going faster than he had expected, and every week he caught himself doing sums instead of listening to his own hands.

Ms. Kang came in carrying two glasses of water and set one on the small table beside the bench. "You're early," she said.

"I counted the keys," he said. "There are eighty-eight. Fifty-two white, thirty-six black."

"Is that useful information?"

"I don't know yet."

She laughed at that, a short genuine sound, and opened the notebook where she kept his assignments in her small exact handwriting. Nicholas had spent the week split between two ways of practicing, and he hadn't told her about the split. In the mornings he drilled the notes exactly as written, fingering marked, metronome set, the discipline his father would recognize and approve. In the evenings, when the house was quiet, he closed the book and hunted for the melody by ear, wrong and slow, letting his hands find shapes the page had never suggested. The morning work was glacial in its progress and somehow felt like lying. The evening work felt true and sounded like nothing.

Solomon, who had taken lessons since he was seven and had become something of an iconoclast about it, told him the page was a cage. "Reading is other people's hands on you," Solomon had said on the bus, tapping the sheet music Nicholas had spread across both their laps. But Ms. Kang, when Nicholas finally described the two practices, his voice climbing into the awkward register it found whenever he admitted to wanting something, did not take Solomon's side or his father's.

"Play me the evening version," she said. "The one you found yourself."

He played it badly. That was the plain truth of it. The right hand wandered off the melody his ear had promised him, and the left hand, asked to hold down two ideas at once, went silent and let the whole thing collapse into single notes. He could feel his face heating. Ms. Kang did not stop him, and she did not lie about it either.

"You found the shape of it," she said. "The shape is good. Now the shape needs walls. What you're doing by ear is not wrong, but it's not finished, because your hands can only do what they've already done. The page isn't a cage. It's other people's hands, yes, but hands that solved problems you haven't met yet." She turned his book toward him. "Same piece. But this week, learn it both ways. Read it until you know it, then close the book and let it go wrong, and listen to where it goes wrong. The going wrong is the lesson."

Nicholas wrote the assignment in his own notebook, and the two records of it sat there side by side, hers exact and his cramped. He was not sure the two practices could live in the same week. He was not sure the counting and the hunting by ear were the same activity at all, or whether fifty-two and thirty-six, neat as they were, had anything to do with the sound that had come out of the attic that night. He only knew he would try both, and that he had four lessons left before September, and that the money in the envelope in his desk had thinned to eleven weeks.

He closed the lid gently over the eighty-eight keys, the way you close a door on someone sleeping.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
Nicole had spread the two articles across her grandmother's dining table, which was vast enough that the printouts did not overlap even when she turned them sideways to compare the abstracts. Both were about whether later school start times improved adolescent attention, and both had arrived through the library database on the same afternoon, looking equally authoritative in their dense columns of text. Her grandmother moved through the room with a watering can, pausing at the fern by the window, and asked what Nicole was reading that required so much sighing.

"The same thing twice," Nicole said, tapping the first page of each. "That's the whole assignment. I have to say which one makes the better case, and why, in eight hundred words." The assignment sheet, folded into quarters beside a saucer of walnuts, called it a critical review, and Mr. Gagnon had told the class that the word critical did not mean hostile; it meant weighing. Nicole liked that idea, the image of two claims set on opposite pans of a scale, though so far both pans felt exactly level, and her draft was stalled at a single sentence she kept deleting.

The writing club met that evening in the same house, because Nicole's grandmother had offered the sunroom to whoever wanted a table and lemonade in July, and so Keenan and Harmony arrived at seven with their own drafts, and the fan, and a laptop that Keenan opened before he had finished sitting down. He read Nicole's opening paragraph aloud in his ceremonial voice, the one he used for other people's sentences, and then he leaned over the table and looked at the articles themselves.

"Easy," he said. "This one wins." He pointed at the article from the journal with the bigger number printed beside its title in the database listing. "Higher impact factor. It means more people cited it, so it's the better journal, so it's the better article. Done, congratulations, go to bed."

Nicole frowned at the screen. "Wait. What does that number actually count?" She typed into the library's help pages, keyboard loud under the fan, and found the definition faster than she expected, sitting there in a paragraph small enough to miss. She read it twice. "It's the average number of citations received in one year by the articles the journal published in the previous two years. That's all. It's about the whole journal, averaged, and it's about the past."

"So more citations means better," Keenan said, but with less force, because Nicole had turned the laptop toward him and was tracing the sentence with her finger.

"It means more cited. It's a count, not a grade." She sat back and looked at the two printouts again, and something about them shifted slightly, the way the dining table had shifted when she'd finally noticed the watermark of ferns pressed into the wood. "This one, the big journal, averaged all its articles over two years and got that number. But I'm not reviewing all its articles. I'm reviewing this one, by these authors, this once." Harmony, who had been peeling an orange into a single unbroken spiral, said that it sounded like judging a whole orchard by the price of fruit at one stand, and Nicole laughed and wrote that down in the margin.

"But it's not nothing, either," Nicole said slowly, because she could feel the pendulum swinging too far the other way, toward dismissing the number entirely, and that felt dishonest too. A journal where lots of articles get cited is a journal people are reading and arguing with, and that counts for something, even if it can't tell you whether this particular argument is built well. She pulled the draft toward her and, underneath the sentence she kept deleting, wrote a question instead: what would make one study better, apart from where it landed?

The answer, when she went looking for it, was quieter than she expected. The big-journal article had surveyed four thousand students, which was impressive, but it had measured attention with a single self-report question, and its discussion section wandered, letting the authors expatiate on policy and parenting until Nicole had lost the thread of their own findings. The small-journal article had three hundred students, but a smarter design: two different measures, taken before and after the schedule change, and a limitation section so frank it was almost painful to read, admitting what the study could not see. She remembered Mr. Gagnon saying that a scholar who names the edges of her knowledge is easier to trust than one who pretends there are no edges.

"Why do they call it a review, though?" Harmony asked, gathering her orange peel into a knot. "Like a movie review?" Nicole considered this, the way she had once considered the etymology of thesis in the middle of a Latin quiz, which her teacher had called a distraction and Nicole had privately called the interesting part. Re-view, she thought. To see again. Not to hand down a verdict but to look at the thing a second time, with someone else's eyes beside your own, and say what you now see. She said none of this out loud. She said, "Because you have to look twice, I think," and reached for the pen.

By ten the sunroom had gone dim except for the lamp over the table, and her grandmother had stopped pretending not to listen from the kitchen doorway. Nicole's draft was three paragraphs long, and the last one said that the smaller study was the stronger piece of scholarship, that the larger journal's reputation told her almost nothing about the article in front of her, and that she still was not certain whether a four-thousand-student survey could outweigh a flaw in its one measure of attention; that she had weighed it and it had not settled. She read the paragraph aloud to Keenan and Harmony, waiting for one of them to object.

Keenan closed the laptop halfway, thinking. "So the number's just a number." Nicole nodded, and her grandmother set down a plate of sliced peaches between the printouts, right on top of the database listing, so that the impact factor disappeared under the fruit.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The car smelled of tatami and cigarettes, the smell of her grandfather's house transferred somehow into her aunt's white sedan, and Victoria sat in the back seat holding the paper lantern in her lap like a sleeping animal. Her aunt drove. Her mother rode in front, silent in a way that was not peaceful. Through the window the town of her mother's childhood slid past in the dusk, tiled roofs, a vending machine glowing blue, and Victoria thought about how she had spent exactly eleven days of her life with the man whose photograph now sat on the family altar, and how that number felt both like nothing and like it should have been enough.

"He would have liked that you came," her aunt said in Japanese, and her mother translated without being asked, in a voice worn thin from translating all week. Victoria nodded. She had texted Daisy a photo of the altar that morning, the small fire her uncle kept lit, and Daisy had replied with three flame emojis and the question, are you okay, and Victoria had started to type the honest answer, which was that she didn't know yet, and deleted it in favor of a thumbs up.

They parked on the gravel shoulder above the river. Down the bank, families were crouched at the water's edge, and small flames moved along the current like a slow procession. Her uncle was already there, waiting beside a shallow wooden tray. Earlier that day Victoria had asked him, in her careful classroom Japanese, whether she could have one of the lanterns, and he had laughed and said something to her mother, and her mother had said, "He says you don't requisition one from the household, you write your name on the household's, it's ours together," and that had settled it, though it had also unsettled something, because she had wanted her own.

Her mother took her arm as they came down the bank, the first time all week she had touched her on purpose. "You know what the fire was for," she said. "At the house. The one your uncle lit the first night." Victoria said she didn't, not really, and her mother looked ahead at the river. "At Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home," she said. "And at the end, they float lanterns down the river to guide the spirits back." That was all. Her mother had never explained anything twice when Victoria was growing up either; she believed you heard a thing once or you didn't.

They knelt on the flat stones. The lantern had her grandfather's name brushed down its side in ink, and beneath it, in smaller characters, the names of ancestors Victoria had never heard of, a whole lineage riding under his. Her uncle struck the match. Watching the flame take hold of the candle stub, Victoria felt something she was almost ashamed of, a lift of exhilaration, a brightness that had no business at a death, and she looked sideways at her mother to see whether her mother felt it too. Her mother's face was closed. Maybe it was only Victoria. Maybe it was wrong. Or maybe it was what the festival was for, this carrying of grief like a lit thing you walk with instead of a weight you kneel under.

Collin had texted her from home: say something to him, like out loud, that's what I'd do. Collin talked to the dead grandfather he'd actually known, casually, on the drive to school. Victoria had thought the advice facile until this moment. Now she crouched with the lantern in both hands at the water's edge and found that there was nothing casual available to her. She said, in English, quietly, "I don't know what to call you." The water pulled. Her uncle touched her shoulder, meaning let go, and she let the lantern down onto the current, and it turned once, caught the pull, and went.

They stood watching it join the others, a hundred small fires going down the dark river, and Victoria's mother finally spoke. "When I was sixteen I fought with him the whole summer before I left for America," she said. "I thought I'd come back the next year and finish the fight. There was no next year." Victoria looked at her. All week her mother had been a closed door, and here in the dark she was saying this to the river, or to her, or to neither. Victoria wanted to ask whether her mother thought the lantern was really going anywhere, whether she believed the spirits traveled or whether this was only a beautiful thing people did, and she understood that the question would be a cruelty dressed up as curiosity.

Back in the car, her aunt turned the ignition and the headlights swept the gravel. Her mother rode with her forehead against the window, watching the river recede. Victoria took out her phone. Daisy had written, how was it, and Victoria began several answers and watched herself not send any of them. "Do you want to stop for ramen," her aunt asked in Japanese, and her mother translated, adding, "She's being facetious, she wants to feed us, that's how she grieves," and Victoria, surprising herself, said, "Tell her yes."

At the intersection her aunt waited for the light, engine idling, and through the windshield Victoria could still see, far down the valley, the faint scattered lights of the lanterns on the water, going where they were going.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Concussion guidelines say an athlete with a suspected concussion should not return to play on the same day, even if they feel fine.
story:
The park had two soccer fields, a drained paddleball court, and a rectangle of asphalt the city had painted with hockey lines, which was where the summer ball hockey league played its Tuesday games. Robert had signed up in May mostly because his mother said an idle summer would disenfranchise him from his own life, an argument he had found vague then and found vague still, though by July he had to admit he liked the league, liked the sound of the ball off the boards his father had helped bolt to the concrete, liked knowing where to be. Mr. Yip, who ran the hardware store on Grand Avenue and had coached the league for eleven years, kept a folding chair behind the net and a spare water bottle for whoever forgot one.

In the second period of the last game of the season, Robert went into the corner with Grace for a loose ball and took a shoulder that put him down harder than he expected. He sat on the asphalt for a moment. The lights hadn't come on yet, and the maples at the edge of the park were doing that late-evening thing where they held the light longer than the ground did. Mr. Yip waved the play dead and skated out, or rather walked out, since it was ball hockey and everyone was in running shoes.

"I'm fine," Robert said, before anyone asked.

"That's not the question I'm asking," Mr. Yip said.

The question, it turned out, was a short list. Where are we? Who's winning? What day is it? Robert answered all three correctly, easily, and felt a small pride in the ease, which should have warned him. His head ached the way a hand aches after you close it in a drawer: not blinding, just insistent, arriving in pulses. Mr. Yip took his elbow and walked him to the folding chair.

"You're done for tonight," Mr. Yip said.

"There's a whole period left. It's tied." Robert heard his own voice go thin. "I feel fine. I answered your questions."

Madisyn, who kept stats in a spiral notebook and had driven three of them to every game, crouched next to the chair. "My cousin plays juniors up north. They drilled it into him. The guidelines say if they suspect a concussion, you don't go back in the same day, even if you feel fine. Even if you feel completely fine. It's not a judgment call."

"It's rec league," Robert said. "In a park."

"You got checked into a board," Madisyn said. "That's a hit at any level."

Robert sat with that. Grace skated over during the break, tapped his knee with her stick, and said, "We can tie it out without you," which was either comfort or an insult, and with Grace was probably both. He watched the third period from the chair, and what he noticed was how much he wanted to be out there, how the wanting had an almost physical pull, the way a muscle remembers a movement. He had always thought of himself as a reasonable person, someone who could weigh a small present pleasure against a large future one, and here was the present pleasure pulling on him like tide.

He also noticed something he hadn't expected. Sitting out, he could see the whole shape of the game, the way Madisyn's cousin's coaches must see it, where the ball should go two passes before it went there. It was interesting. It was also a little humiliating, because a part of him suspected he liked the view, and that liking was a dilettante's liking, a spectator's, the kind you earn by giving something up. He couldn't decide whether sitting still and watching was a kind of wisdom or a kind of cowardice dressed as one, and he suspected the honest answer was that he wouldn't know until morning, when the headache either was there or wasn't. His cousin's rule, the rule Madisyn had recited, treated him like a person who couldn't be trusted to report on himself, and it stung, and it also matched the evidence, because he had said I feel fine twice and both times had meant it and both times had been wrong. He decided he could hold both of those at once: the rule was right, and it took something from him that only he could name.

After the game, which they lost by one, on a shot that banked in off the far post, Mr. Yip folded the chair and carried it to the trunk of his car with the spare water bottle still cold under his arm. The maples had let go of the light, and the lamps along the path had come on, and moths were working the lamps in their steady, affective, purposeless way, so devoted to the light that Robert felt a little sorry for them.

Madisyn closed her notebook. "Ride home?"

"In a minute," Robert said. He stood, carefully, the way you test a floorboard, and the asphalt stayed where it was. Then he picked up his stick and carried it to the boards, and leaned it there with the others.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Sustained Investigation section asks for 15 digital images and counts for 60 percent of the score.
story:
Dominic had arranged his sketchbook, three pencils, a gum eraser, and a printed checklist on the kitchen table in a way that he felt communicated seriousness, the way a general might arrange maps before an invasion. The checklist said, in his own handwriting, TEN PIECES. ONE THEME. ARTIST'S STATEMENT, 300 WORDS. Below that he had written possible themes: doors, hands, empty pools, my grandfather's handwriting. He had underlined "empty pools" twice, which meant nothing, since he had also crossed it out twice.

Tommy arrived with a grocery bag of sour candy and no invitation, which was standard. He dropped into the chair across from Dominic and read the checklist upside down, an impressive but useless skill. "Ten pieces," he said. "That's a lot of pools."

"They're not pools anymore. I'm deciding."

"You've been deciding since September. It's October. Soon it'll be November and you'll be deciding in a cold, serious way." Tommy ate a candy with the phlegmatic calm of someone who had never once had a deadline. Dominic pointed out, not for the first time, that Tommy had taken cooking as his elective and his only portfolio was a lasagna. Tommy said the lasagna had been a sustained investigation of cheese, and Dominic threw the eraser at him, and it went under the radiator, and Tommy made no move to retrieve it because the eraser had absconded, he said, into witness protection.

The real trouble arrived with Darius, who was a senior and had come by to return a ladder, or possibly to escape his own house, where his mother was repainting the hallway in a color called "gentle fawn" that had made everyone in his family quiet and strange. Darius sat down, looked at the checklist, and made a sound through his teeth that Dominic recognized as the sound of bad news.

"What," Dominic said.

"Where'd you get ten?" Darius asked. "Ten pieces."

"Ms. Shapiro. She said ten artworks around one theme. That's the portfolio."

Darius pulled out his phone, thumbed through his camera roll, and turned the screen around. It was a photo of a page from the AP course description he'd screenshotted last year, when he'd made the opposite mistake and panicked in the other direction. "Look at the actual thing," he said, and tapped the screen with one finger. "The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio. The Sustained Investigation section wants fifteen digital images."

"Fifteen," Dominic repeated. The word sat on the kitchen table like a dropped plate.

"And it's not a small part," Darius said. "It counts for sixty percent of the score." He said this in the flat tone of someone quoting scripture he had personally suffered under, and then he stole a candy.

Dominic read the screenshot twice, once fast and once slow, the way you reread a text message you hope will change. He had built his whole autumn around ten. Ten was a number you could hold in your head, a hand span and a thumb. Fifteen was a different animal, an animal with five more legs.

Tommy, chewing, said, "Could you just photograph them from two angles?"

"That's not how it works," Dominic and Darius said together, and then looked at each other with the mild suspicion of people who had never agreed before.

Dominic sat with it. His first instinct was to treat the extra five as a punishment, five extra miles on a run. But something about Darius's screenshot kept pulling at him, and he turned his sketchbook to the page of crossed-out pools, then to the page of doors, then to the page of his grandfather's handwriting, which he had copied off an old postcard: weather turning, take the long way home. He noticed, for the first time, that he had drawn doors in the margins of the handwriting page and handwriting on the doors page, and that maybe these were not three themes but one, doors and letters both being things that open or stay shut. He did not say this out loud, because out loud it sounded like something a person with a beret would say, but he wrote it down: doors, what passes through them, what doesn't.

"So you're not doing pools," Tommy said, reading upside down again.

"The pools were never really pools. I don't even like pools."

"You went to Milly Kowalczyk's pool party for six hours."

"Her cousin's pool. And that's different. That was social."

Darius laughed and stood up to go reclaim his ladder, pausing at the door to say that if Dominic actually did the fifteen, Ms. Shapiro would probably frame something of his in the hallway outside the art room, which was a recompense Dominic privately considered worth more than the score itself, though he'd never admit that either. After the door closed, Tommy slid the last candy across the table like a man paying a debt, and Dominic took it and started a new checklist.

At the top he wrote FIFTEEN IMAGES, and underlined it once, and then, in smaller letters, SIXTY PERCENT, and then, in letters so small they were almost a secret, what my grandfather would write through a closed door.

"Some artist's statement," Tommy said, peering at it.

"It's a draft," Dominic said, and turned the page.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013 for $250 million.
story:
Victoria had the laptop balanced on the arm of the couch, a Washington Post article open about warehouse workers and heat waves, when Brittany dropped onto the cushion beside her and read over her shoulder.

"You're doing homework on a Friday," Brittany said. "In the living room. That's genuinely sad."

"It's for Mr. Chea's class. We have to find an article about a big company and evaluate it." Victoria scrolled down. The article was careful, well reported, full of numbers about productivity quotas. Something about it had been bothering her for twenty minutes, and she hadn't yet found the shape of the bother.

Ajay came in from the kitchen with a bowl of cereal and sat on the floor. "Which company?"

"Amazon."

"Amazon," Ajay repeated, and spooned up milk. "You know who owns that paper, right?"

"The Washington Post? The Graham family." She had learned that somewhere, the way she had learned that Gutenberg invented the printing press, a fact with no weight attached to it.

"Since 2013, no. Jeff Bezos bought it from them. Two hundred and fifty million dollars." Ajay said it the way he said most things, flat, like he was reading a license plate. "The Amazon guy."

Victoria looked at the article again. The warehouse workers. Amazon. The man who owned both. "Wait," she said. "So the person the paper is reporting on owns the paper."

"Basically, yeah."

Brittany leaned back. "So it's fake, then. It's all fake, everything's bought, nothing matters." She said it cheerfully, the way she said most things, but Victoria noticed she kept scrolling with one finger, not leaving.

"No, that's not..." Victoria stopped. She was thinking of her mother, who transliterated the headlines from her Khmer news app into English out loud at breakfast, converting them sound by sound into something her daughter could hold, and who trusted them all the more because of the effort. Her mother was not naive. She simply believed that if you worked hard enough at a text, the text would tell you the truth. Victoria had always liked believing that too.

"Mr. Chea would say you're overcorrecting," Ajay said. "If everything is bought, then the word bought stops meaning anything."

"I'm not saying everything is bought. I'm saying this one is." Victoria clicked to another tab and typed. The Post's own site said it plainly, in a page about its history: sold to Bezos in 2013, from the Graham family, $250 million. She read it twice. It was strange to see the fact sitting there so quietly, like a connoisseur's signature in the corner of a painting, small and decisive, changing the value of everything around it once you noticed it.

"So what do we do with that?" Brittany asked. "Cross it out? Write 'owned by Amazon' on the printout and hand that in?"

Victoria was quiet for a moment. "No. I was going to write that the article is compromised and leave it there. That was the whole plan, honestly. Five paragraphs of that."

"And now?"

"Now I think that's lazy." She pulled the laptop back onto her knees and started rereading the piece, slower this time, watching what the reporter had actually done. There were interviews with workers. There were documents. There was a line, acerbic and precise, about the company's internal temperature monitoring that she had skimmed past the first time and that now seemed almost defiant, a small sharp thing left out in the open. The paper had been sold, and yet someone inside it had gone on asking questions. Both of those things were true at once, and she did not know yet how much weight to give each one, and she wrote that down too, at the bottom of her notes, with a question mark after it.

"Half an hour," Brittany said, checking her phone. "Then we're getting food."

"Half an hour." Victoria typed her first line: The Washington Post has been owned by Jeff Bezos since 2013, when he bought it from the Graham family for $250 million, and this article is about Amazon, and I am not sure what follows from that.

Ajay set his empty bowl on the coffee table and leaned over to read her screen. "That's your opening sentence?"

"That's my opening sentence."

He was quiet, then nodded slowly. "It's honest, at least."

Victoria kept typing.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
On the night before his third attempt, Cameron sat at the kitchen table with the driver's handbook open to the chapter on parking, while his mother washed lettuce at the sink and pretended not to hover. The overhead light laid a flat glare across the pages, and a thin spill of sugar, alluvial, had drifted from the bowl toward the book's spine where his elbow had disturbed it. Two fails already. The first for a merge onto the parkway that his examiner had described, in red ink, as tentative to the point of hazard; the second for a parallel park that had eviscerated a row of cones in a way Cameron still did not fully understand. He wanted the license before September, before orientation, before the apartment in the city where a car would be useless but the freedom of having one would not.

"Read it out loud," his mother said. "You remember things better out loud."

"Downhill, next to a curb," he read, and stopped. The sentence went on about wheels, but the words kept sliding past him, the way the whole chapter on hills had slid past him for two weeks. He copied the sentence onto an index card instead, then copied it again, then turned the card over and tried to write it from memory and got the wheels facing the wrong way.

Lucian picked him up the next morning in his uncle's sedan, a car with a body like a bruised plum and a driver's seat adjusted for someone twice Lucian's size. Nelson came too, wedged in the back with a bag of chips, having declared himself the designated evaluator, a position for which he demanded remuneration and accepted, after negotiation, one slushie, medium, blue. They drove to Sycamore Street, where the curb ran along a slope long and steady enough that a parked car could dream about rolling.

"Okay," Lucian said. "Park behind the blue hatchback. Show me the person who failed you doesn't exist."

The first tries were ugly. Cameron came in too fast and had to reset, then too wide, then he clipped the imaginary cone zone Nelson invented on the spot and narrated mercilessly. On the fifth attempt he slid in clean, tires hugging the curb, the hatchback's bumper a polite hand-width from his own. He sat back, exhaling, and reached to shift out of gear, and felt the car lean, very slightly, a suggestion of motion downhill toward the intersection at the bottom of the street.

He stopped with his hand on the gearshift. Which way were the wheels pointing right now? He looked down through the windshield as if he could see them, which of course he could not, and understood that he had never once, in all his practice, thought about the wheels after the parking was over. The card in his pocket facedown in his memory, wrong-facing. He turned the steering wheel slowly and felt for the tires against the curb.

"What are you doing?" Nelson asked, leaning between the seats. "You passed. It's over. Celebrate."

"Wait." Cameron eased off the brake and let the car drift an inch, and the front tire kissed the curb with a soft, certain tap, and the car stopped. He sat looking at that for a moment, the little tap still in his ears. Turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail, he said, mostly to himself. He tried it the other way, wheels out, just to see, and the car leaned its whole body toward the street like something considering leaving. He turned them back. "Okay," he said. "Now it's over."

They spent another hour on it, park after park on the slope, until the wheel direction came as fast as the blinker, and then Lucian drove them to the merge ramp and made Cameron take it three times at highway speed, Nelson calling out gaps in traffic like a spotter. On the morning of the test, Cameron did everything the same way: the park on the practice hill was clean, the merge was decisive, the examiner made a small check mark and said congratulations.

He drove home licensed, alone, and pulled in behind his mother's car at the curb on their own sloped street, turned his wheels toward the curb out of pure habit, and sat there feeling the day settle. His mother came out in her slippers with the mail in her hand, looked at his front wheels angled against the curb, and frowned.

"Honey, straighten those," she said. "You'll wear the tires crooked."
